translations.text: Lamentation came there, and the idols fell. The day was glorious over the earth when the multitude set out.
(Their lands were covered with a helmet of cloud), border-dwellings on the moorland slopes. Moses led the army over them, past many dangers [?].
They were forced into narrow northern paths. They knew that to the south of them lay the land of the Ethiopians, hill-slopes scorched, a people browned by the hot coals of heaven.
There holy God shielded the people against the sudden burning. He spread a canopy over the burning sky, a holy net over the hot air.

Onward they saw the guide of life measure out the way of life. The sky ruled their journey, and the seafarers followed along the flood-way. The people were in joy, and loud was the clamour of the host.
A heavenly beacon rose every evening, another wonder. After the sun had gone down its setting-course, it was seen, strangely, shining with flame over the people: a burning pillar.
Clear beams stood bright over the warriors. The shields shone and the shadows vanished. The deep shadows of night could not hide their hiding-places nearby. The candle of heaven burned.

A new night-guard had of necessity to keep watch over the troops, so that the terror of the wilderness, the grey heath-terror, with its ocean-like storms, should not cut off their lives in a sudden grip.
The one going before had fiery locks and bright beams. With hot flame it threatened the war-band with a terror [?] that it would burn up the host in the wilderness, unless they bravely obeyed Moses.

The bright host shone and the shields gleamed. The shield-warriors saw the straight road and the sign above the troops, until the sea-fortress at the land's end blocked the way of the people's army, which was eager to go forward.
The camp was set up. The weary men refreshed themselves. The brave servers brought food to them, and they restored their strength.
After the trumpet sang, the seafarers spread out their tents along the hills. That was the fourth camp, the resting place of the shield-warriors, by the Red Sea.

There sudden news came into their army, terror from inland. Fear arose, the dread of slaughter among the hosts. The exile awaited the hateful pursuer, who long before had imposed hardship on them, the homeless ones, and bound them in woe with torments.
They did not heed the covenant, though the elder king had once become guardian [?] of the native peoples, of men, in return for treasures [?], so that he prospered so greatly [?].
They forgot all this after the race of the Egyptians grew angry over a dispute [?]. Then they committed murder against his kinsmen, contrived accusations, and broke the covenant.

The surges of hostility lay close to their hearts, the passion of the men. With wicked faithlessness they meant to repay that reward for life with treachery, so that the people of Moses should pay for that day's work with blood, where mighty God had granted them success on that journey of destruction.

Then the courage of the men turned to despair once they saw Pharaoh's army coming on from the southern ways, carrying their forest of spears, the troop glittering (spears were arrayed, the battle moved on,

the shield-covers gleamed, the trumpets sang), the banners [?] resound, the nation tread the border, on [?] … The war-birds cried out, greedy for battle and dewy-feathered, over the corpses of the host [?]: the dark chooser of the slain.
The wolves sang a terrible evening song in hope of food. Those careless beasts, bold at killing, waited on the track of the hated ones for the fall of the people's army.
The border-guards cried out in the middle of the night. The doomed spirit fled, and the people were hemmed in.
At times proud thanes from that host measured out the miles on horseback.
There the king with the standard, the prince of men, rode at their head beside the standard with the border-troop.

The war-leader of men fastened his grim helmet, the king his chin-guard (banners glittered), expecting battle. He shook his coat of mail and ordered his chosen troop to hold the battle formation firmly. With hostile eyes the friends [?] watched the coming of the people of the land.
Fearless warriors moved around him. The grey war-wolves, thirsty for the clash of war and loyal to their lord, greeted the battle.
He had chosen for himself two thousand glorious men from the nobility of the people. They were kings and close kinsmen, by that [?] right, and dear for their noble birth.
Therefore each one led out every warrior of the male sex that he could find in that time.
They were all native men [?] together, kings in the company. Often the familiar horn summoned [?] in the throng to which [?] the young warriors, the war-band of men, bore their gear [?].
So there the dark host [?] led [?], foe after foe, a great number of the people's army, by thousands. They were eager to go there.
With those mighty troops they had resolved at dawn to cut down the race of Israel with swords, in vengeance for their brothers.
So weeping was raised up in the camps, a terrible evening song. Terrors stood around, and the death-net [?] held them when the uproar came.

Dire tidings flew. The enemy was resolute and the host was bright with weapons, until the mighty angel who guarded the multitude thrust back the proud ones, so that the foes could no longer see each other there. Their paths were divided.
The fugitives had the space of a night, though enemies lurked on every side of them, an army on one side and the sea on the other. They had no other way out.
They had lost hope of their rightful homeland. They sat along the hills in shining [?] garments, expecting woe. The whole band of kinsmen waited together, keeping watch, for the greater force,

until Moses ordered the men at dawn, with brazen trumpets, to gather the people: the warriors were to rise, take up their coats of mail, set their minds on courage, carry their bright armour, and call the troop with signals nearer to the sand.
Quickly the watchmen remembered the war-song, and the host was urged on. The seafarers took up their tents over the hills [?] (they heard the trumpets). The army was in haste.
Then they counted out twelve troops of brave men in the vanguard against that hateful foe. The army was stirred up.

From each tribe of that noble race, fifty companies of the people's nobility were chosen under the shields for the muster. Each company had [?] hundred glorious men counted from a famous troop of spear-bearers and warriors.
That was a warlike host. The leaders of the army did not admit the weak into that count of warriors.

those who because of their youth could not yet, under the cover of shields, defend the mail-shirts of men against the treacherous foe with their hands, and had not yet suffered a deadly wound over the rim of a shield, a grievous bodily wound, in the boastful play of the spear.

The old, the grey battle-warriors, were not allowed to fight in the battle if their strength had faded among the brave troops. Instead they chose men for war by their stature, and by how well courage with honour, together with strength and the grip on the spear-shaft, would hold out in the nation.

Then the army of hand-brave men was together, eager to go forward. The banner rose up, brightest of beams. All of them still waited until the messenger of the journey, a light over the shields near the sea-streams, broke through the doors of the air.
Then the battle-caller leapt up before the heroes, the bold herald [?]. He raised up his shield and ordered the leaders of the people to quiet the army while many listened to the brave man's speech.
This is the eternal God of Abraham, Lord of creation, who protects this army, brave and mighty, with his great hand."
They did not take to heart the teaching of the holy one at all, after the song of the beloved one [?] nearer the end [?], when the sound and the mingled singing died away.

Then the fourth tribe went first and waded into the waves, warriors in a band, over the green sea-floor. The troop of Judah, alone in the vanguard [?], went onto the unknown path ahead of its kinsmen.
After that army the seafarers grew bold, the sons of Reuben. The sea-warriors carried their shields over the salt marsh, a multitude of men. A great single troop went on unafraid.

After them came the sons of Simeon, marching on in their tribes and companies. The third great nation pressed forward as a picked war-band, dewy with spear-shafts, while banners waved above the advancing spears.

Each man knew the law of the kindreds and the noble descent of his people, as Moses had told them. They had one father, a beloved founder of the nation, wise in spirit and dear to his kinsmen, who had received the right to the land.
Noah, the glorious prince, sailed with his three sons over new floods: the deepest of the drowning floods that ever came about in the kingdom of the world.
So wise men say in their words that Abraham's father was the ninth from Noah in the count of the generations.
That is the Abraham for whom the God of angels created a new name. Besides that, he committed holy hosts near and far into his keeping, and power over the nations. He lived in exile.
Afterwards, at the command of the Holy One, he led the one whose life was dearest to him. The kinsmen climbed the high land, up onto the mountain of Zion.
There they found the covenant and saw glory, the holy, exalted pledge, as men have heard tell.
There, later, the wise son of David, the glorious king, following the teachings of the prophet, built a temple to God, a holy shrine. He was the wisest of earthly kings in the kingdom of the world,
and it was the highest and holiest, the most famous among men, the greatest and most glorious of all that the children of men, people throughout the earth, have made with their hands.
Abraham led his son Isaac to that meeting place. The fire of the pyre was kindled. The first slayer of life was none the gladder for it.

He was willing to give his heir to the flame, in the blaze of the pyre, the best of men, his dear son, as a victory-offering. The boy was his only heir on earth and the comfort of his life, the long-lasting hope he had waited so long for as a legacy to his people.

He showed this when he seized the boy firmly with his hands. The man renowned among the people drew the ancient heirloom, his sword (the blade roared). He showed that he held his own life no dearer than obedience to the King of heaven.
Then Abraham rose up. The warrior meant to slay his son, still not grown, and redden his kinsman with the edge of the sword, if the Lord let him.
The bright Father did not want to take the child, the holy offering, from him, but held him back with his hand.
Then a voice came from heaven to restrain him, a glorious sound, and spoke these words: "Do not slay your own child with the sword, Abraham, your son!

The truth has been made known, now that the King of all creatures has tested you: you have kept faith with the Ruler, firm trust. That shall be your peace for as long as you live, forever and always, unfailing.
What greater pledge could a son of man need?

Heaven and earth cannot encompass the word of his glory. It is wider and broader than the corners of the earth can embrace, wider than the circle of the world and the heavens above, the expanse of the ocean and this sad air.

He swears an oath by his own life, the Prince of angels, Ruler of fates and God of hosts, true Lord of victories: that men across the earth will not know the number of your race and kin, your shield-warriors,

nor be able by any skill to tell it in true words, unless someone becomes so wise in mind that he alone can count all the stones on earth, the stars in heaven, the sand of the sea-dunes and the salt waves.
But they shall settle between the two seas, as far as the foreign people [?] of Egypt, in the land of the Canaanites: your people, the father's noble children, the best of nations."
The people were afraid. Terror of the flood came over their sad spirits. The ocean threatened death.
The mountain slopes were drenched with blood, and the sea spewed out gore. There was an outcry on the waves. The water was full of weapons, and a mist of death rose up.
The Egyptians were turned back and fled in fear. They saw the sudden danger, and in their panic the army wanted to get home. Their boasting turned to grief.

The terrible rolling of the waves closed darkly over them. None of the army came home, because fate locked them in from behind with the wave. Where paths had lain before, the sea raged. The host was drowned.
The waters rose up, and a storm of sound went up high to heaven, the greatest cry of an army.
The hated enemy cried out with doomed voices (the air above grew dark). Blood spread through the flood.
The shield-walls were broken. The sky lashed down the greatest of sea-deaths. The brave died, kings among their troops. At the sea's edge their hope of return [?] failed.
Battle-shields shone high above the men. The sea-wall rose, the raging sea-stream. The host was firmly fettered in death, and their way forward was cunningly blocked. The sands awaited

the doomed army, until the stream of the waves, the ever-cold sea with its salt waves, used to wandering paths [?], came to seek its everlasting foundations. It was a naked messenger of distress, a hostile marching spirit, and it overwhelmed the enemies.

The blue air was mixed with gore. The bursting sea threatened the seafarers' journey with bloody terror, until the true Lord, through Moses' hand, set the raging water free [?]. It hunted far and wide and swept them away in its deadly embrace.

The proud nations could not hold back the path of the helpers [?] or the fury of the sea-current. With its screaming terror it struck down many. The ocean raged; it rose up, then slid down. Terrors stood, and the death-wounds welled.

The flood-pale army, held fast all around, gave up their souls [?] after the dark surge came down on them, the greatest of the raging waves. The whole host perished when the Egyptian force was drowned, Pharaoh together with his peoples.
Then, on the shore of the sea, Moses, the man of high excellence, spoke eternal counsels to the Israelites: holy speech, a profound message.
He shines more light on us now that scholars tell us better of the longer joys of life. This joy here is fleeting. It is cursed with sins, granted to exiles, a time of waiting for the wretched.
"Great is this multitude. Strong is the leader of hosts, the greatest of helpers, who leads this journey. Among the race of Canaan he has granted us cities and rings of treasure and a broad kingdom.

Now the Lord of angels intends to fulfil what he long ago promised with an oath to the race of your fathers in days of old. If you keep the holy teaching, you will go on to overcome every one of your enemies. You will possess a victorious kingdom between the seas, the beer-halls of men. Great will be your glory!"

After those words the host was joyful. The trumpets of victory sang with a fair sound, and the banners stood raised. The people were on land. The beam of glory had led the host, the holy companies, into God's keeping [?].
They rejoiced in their lives, now that they had brought them out of the power of their enemies. They had dared it boldly, these men beneath the roofs of the waters.
They saw the walls standing there. All the seas through which they had carried their war-gear seemed bloody to them.
Then it was easy to find African women on the shore of the ocean, adorned with gold.
